title: The king who said no
hookLine: Shantanu falls for the fisherman's daughter but won't give away his son's crown: kama honored, inside dharma
carry: kama is honored, but dharma comes first
last: KNOWLEDGE COMES DOWN FROM GURU TO STUDENT.

lines: HE FOLLOWS IT TO THE WATER.
cards: A scent on the wind, sweet and strong, out by the Yamuna River. King Shantanu is walking in the woods along the bank when he catches it, and he can't tell where it comes from. So he follows it.

It leads him to the water, and to a young woman with a boat, who ferries travelers across. He asks who she is. She's the daughter of the chief of the fishermen, she says, and she plies this boat at her father's bidding.

teach.b: Shantanu wants to marry her. He goes to her father and asks. The fisherman doesn't refuse; his daughter must marry someday, and the king is welcome.
But there's a condition. Promise me, he says, that the son born of her will be king after you. And Shantanu can't.
He already has an heir: Devavrata, Ganga's son, the young man he brought home from the river.

teach.h: HE WON'T TAKE HIS SON'S CROWN.
teach.b: To promise the crown to a son not yet born would mean taking it from the son he has. So the king won't agree, and goes home. Back in the capital he can't stop thinking about her.
He grows quiet and withdrawn, sunk in thought, the text says, and won't tell anyone why. There's a big Hindu teaching inside that silence.
Hinduism names four aims of a human life, the purusharthas: dharma, doing what's right; artha, livelihood and success; kama, love, pleasure and desire; and moksha, freedom. Kama is on the list.
Wanting someone isn't a sin here; it's one of the good things a life is for.

But kama lives inside dharma, not on top of it. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that in living beings he is the desire that doesn't go against dharma. Shantanu's longing is real, and the text doesn't mock it.

teach.h: KAMA IS HONORED, BUT DHARMA COMES FIRST.
teach.b: But his duty as a father comes first: you don't take a son's crown to get what you want. So he carries both, the dharma and the longing, and lets dharma decide.
And the person who will notice first is the son the no was meant to protect.

how: Hindu teachers often describe four aims of life, dharma, artha, kama and moksha, and teach that love and pleasure are good when they are pursued within dharma.

o: Shantanu's promise to marry the woman with the boat
the fisherman's demand that the king give up his throne
a son's great promise, which begins with his father's honorable no

games.q: the four aims of life — tap the pairs.

s: in Hinduism, desire itself is a sin
kama is one of the four aims of life; it belongs inside dharma.
Shantanu agreed to the fisherman's condition
he wouldn't take the crown from Devavrata, and went home.
Shantanu's longing was real, and his duty still came first
he grieved for her in silence, but kept his son's crown safe.

games.q: you're Shantanu. you love the fisherman's daughter. the price is your son's crown. what does dharma ask?
o: promise, and sort it out later.
keep your son's crown and go home.
games.why: he keeps faith with his son and goes home, and he doesn't pretend the longing isn't there. kama is honored; dharma decides.

practice: Bring to mind something you want right now, honestly, without judging it. Breathe in and name it: in Hindu terms that's kama, and it's allowed.

Breathe out and ask the question Shantanu faced: is this in line with my dharma, what's right for me to do in my place? If you pray, offer the wanting to God and ask for a clear heart. You don't have to decide anything now.

wordCard.voice: Bhishma's vow. It begins with a king's refusal: he won't give his son's crown away, even for the woman he wants.

orig.note: Sanskrit kāma, desire, love and pleasure: one of the four aims of life.

carryVoice: Your line: kama is honored, but dharma comes first. Tomorrow, the son notices. That's day seven hundred ten.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Shantanu meets the fisherman's daughter by the Yamuna; the fisherman's condition; the king's grief)
Bhagavad Gita 7.11 (Krishna: in beings I am desire not opposed to dharma)
The four purusharthas (dharma, artha, kama, moksha): standard Hindu teaching
